newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-33 years after, morbid tour recreates JFK murder.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-33 years after, morbid tour recreates JFK murder.

text.p: The elegant open-top Lincoln Continental glides slowly by Dealey Plaza to the sound of cheers and wild applause.
Suddenly, as it approaches the now-notorious grassy knoll, rifle fire cuts the air. The limousine stops, then speeds off to Parkland Hospital with sirens wailing.

Thirty-three years after President John Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas on Nov. 22, 1963, a macabre tour recreating his final moments in gruesome detail is drawing tourists who want to get closer to the murder than a museum exhibit. The "JFK Presidential Limousine Tour" uses a 1964 Lincoln Continental remodeled to match the one that took Kennedy on his fateful journey and the haunting sounds of that day are replayed to tourists over the car's stereo system.

For $25, visitors get a one-hour tour that retraces the route taken by the president and his wife Jacqueline from Love Field airport into the city centre and past the Texas School Book Depositary, where authorities say Lee Harvey Oswald fired on the first couple from a sixth-floor window.

Demand for the tour, which began several months ago, has picked up sharply in advance of the 33rd anniversary of the assassination that changed the course of history and inspired scores of dark conspiracy theories.

As the replica limousine enters Dealey Plaza, its stereo blasts out the sounds of cheering crowds and radio reports from 1963. Then shots ring out and a voice cries "My God, they are going to kill us all" -- the voice of John Connally, who was Texas governor at the time and was wounded in the attack.

When the limousine arrives at Parkland Hospital after a mad dash along a major highway, a sombre radio announcer's voice from 1963 is played, describing the scenes of chaos and giving the tragic news. "President Kennedy has been assassinated ... It's official now. The president is dead."

The tour, lambasted by critics as a tasteless scam that exploits Kennedy's memory to make a quick buck, is the brainchild of Paul Crute, a former Dallas salesman who was just a baby when Kennedy was murdered. Crute, who also drives the limousine, seems genuinely surprised that anyone would take offence and insists that every one of his passengers has said the tour helped them understand what happened here.

"It allows you to relive a pivotal event in history," he said, adding that he uncovered other details of Kennedy's assassination that would have made the tour even more dramatic but did not use them because it would be in "poor taste."
Tacky or not, most customers said the tour is effective.

"It gave me goosebumps, knowing we were on the same route that he (Kennedy) took. It really brings it home," said Elizabeth Jackson, a middle-aged housewife from Wisconsin, who took the tour with her husband during a trip to Dallas.

The image of Kennedy as a charismatic and optimistic figure continues its tight hold on the popular imagination and the mystery of his assassination still burns strong. Many experts doubt the lone assassin theory put up by the official Warren Commission, which concluded that Oswald acted alone.
According to the most popular of the conspiracy theories, a second gunman fired the bullet that killed Kennedy from the grassy knoll to the front and right of the limousine.

Few of the historians, researchers and ordinary citizens who were to gather on the grassy knoll on Friday to honour Kennedy's memory were expected to approve of Crute's limousine tour, although Gary Mack, an expert on the assassination and archivist at the Dallas County Historical Foundation, said the most important thing is that Kennedy is remembered.

"While researchers personally may really despise the tour and some of the more bizarre (conspiracy) theories that come out, they realise that you have to keep up the attention. And this stuff does that," Mack said.
But several people visiting Dallas this week said they found the idea of the limousine tour distateful.

"No, I don't think I'd want to go on that. It cheapens his memory, turns it into a circus," said Maggie Peterson, a New Yorker who was in college when Kennedy was assassinated and has visited the site of his death several times.
Experts say the tour's mere existence illustrates that the Kennedy assassination has become less painful to Americans than it was just a few years ago.

"Something like that would never have happened 10 to 15 years ago because there would have been such an upcry in the community. It just wouldn't have been allowed," said James Pennebaker, a psychologist at Southern Methodist University who has studied the impact of the murder on Dallas residents.
